items.text: SEASON 10 · EPISODE 6 · DRAFT  Coldframe Sound, Studio A · week four · Maya, Corbin, Esme and Pim; Ottilie, the mastering engineer, by phone · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  The single is mastered. Corbin wants it louder. The mastering engineer says it’s already too loud. Both are sure, and only one of them has heard what the playlist does to it.  ⚑ RV-176: the master’s sound is the mastering engineer’s and Esme’s; the spec is the label’s. RV-177: service targets and figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Louder Than Everything
items.stakes: The label wants the single louder than the playlist. The playlist has other plans.
items.reward: A master its owners chose by ear at fair loudness — and no more clipped takes.

items.text: Act I — “The playlist turns it down”

items.prompt: 11:10. Corbin wants it louder; Ottilie says it's already too loud. What first?
unknown: What the playlist does to each
items.risk: A master pushed louder to lose on the playlist.

hints.text: What happens to a loud master when the playlist plays it?

options.label: Push the limiter another 3 dB
options.result: −4 LUFS. The drums become a wall. The service turns it down 10 dB.
options.consequence: More of what made it small.

options.label: Measure both versions' integrated loudness and true peak, then play them loudness-matched the way the service will
options.result: Hot: −7 LUFS, +0.8 dBTP. Dynamic: −12 LUFS. Matched, the dynamic one sounds bigger.

options.label: Tell Corbin loudness doesn't matter any more
options.result: He hears it as a brush-off and goes over your head.
options.consequence: True-ish, and useless without the demonstration.

options.label: Book a different mastering engineer who'll make it louder
options.result: Not your call, and not the problem.
options.consequence: Replaces an owner instead of informing her.

items.title: The playlist turns it down.
items.body: At the service's target (−14 LUFS here) the hot master is turned down 7 dB, the dynamic version only 2. They now play equally loud — and the hot one's choruses are no bigger than its verses; its drums arrive flattened. Corbin listens twice, then says it: ‘The quiet one's bigger.’
items.label: Test: how much further down does the loud one go — and which sounds louder after?

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Corbin and Maya beside a board. It needs to be as loud as everything else on the playlist. Louder. It measures minus seven integrated, with peaks at plus zero point eight. The service plays everything at its own target. So louder isn't louder?

bubbles.text: It needs to be as loud as everything else on the playlist. Louder.

items.text: 📕 WHEN & WHY · MASTERY  Terms   Integrated loudness   Loudness normalization   True peak   LUFS   The situation  The master measures −7 LUFS integrated with true peaks of +0.8 dBTP. The streaming service normalizes every track to its own target (say −14 LUFS). Which relationship tells you what listeners actually get?   Which relationship do you reach for?  Perceived loudness (rule of thumb)  Loudness correction  Decibels to a power ratio     Reference: the 📖 Glossary has every formula. At mastery, knowing  which  and  why  is the skill.

items.label: **Find it:** where did the single go wrong?

items.alt: A loudness sheet. Left: the hot master at −7 LUFS and the dynamic one at −12, with the service's −14 target as a dashed blue line — the hot one turned down 7 dB, the dynamic one 2 dB. Right: short-term loudness across the song after that gain — the hot master's line almost flat around −14; the dynamic one's verses lower and choruses higher.
items.caption: Same loudness. Different song.

items.title: ‘true peak ≤ −1.0 dBTP’
items.body: Page 3 of the label's delivery spec, which nobody had opened: ‘Masters: 24-bit, 48 kHz. True peak not to exceed −1.0 dBTP. Loudness: at the mastering engineer's discretion.’

items.label: **Hear it:** play both masters the way the playlist will.

items.title: Agreeing what ‘loud’ means
items.body: In 1939 American broadcasters and telephone engineers agreed a standard volume indicator — the VU meter — so that everyone reading a needle meant the same thing by ‘how loud’. Its needle was deliberately slow, to follow roughly how loud speech and music feel rather than their fastest peaks. Loudness meters in LUFS are the same argument, eighty years on: measure what people hear.

items.title: Overs after the encoder.
items.body: On a phone stream the hot master crunches on every snare. Its true peak is +0.8 dBTP — between the samples, the waveform goes over full scale, and the lossy encoder makes it worse. The label's spec, page 3, asks for −1.0 dBTP or lower. And Pim's peak logs show where the damage started: two choir takes recorded with peaks pinned at 0 dBFS.
items.label: Test: how far must the peaks come down — and who chooses the master?

items.alt: The control room; a phone on speaker on the console shows ‘Ottilie’; Esme listens, smiling; Corbin looks surprised.

bubbles.text: Give me a master near minus eleven, peaks at minus one. It'll breathe.
That's the one I heard in my head.

items.prompt: Why didn't anyone tell me the playlist turns things down?

options.label: “Because everyone assumes everyone knows. Now you know, and you can tell the next artist.”
options.reply: I'm going to be insufferable about this at the label.

options.label: “It's been that way for years.”
options.reply: Then it's been expensive for years.

items.prompt: −7 LUFS, +0.8 dBTP, turned down 7 dB and crunching on phones. What do you recommend — and to whom?
items.risk: A single that sounds small and crunchy where people hear it.
timeout: The hot master goes to the label.

hints.text: Who owns the master's sound — and what do they need from you?

options.label: Leave it — delivery's Friday
options.consequence: Knowingly ships a master over the spec.

options.label: Take the loudness-matched comparison and the spec to Ottilie and Esme; recommend a master near −11 LUFS with true peaks at −1.0 dBTP; let them choose; the label's spec decides the files
options.result: Ottilie makes it; Esme approves it; Corbin signs the delivery form.
options.consequence: Evidence to the people who own the sound, inside the label's spec.

options.label: Master it to exactly −14 LUFS so nothing gets turned down
options.result: Fine on the playlist — and quiet on the radio edit and in the club, where Esme wanted weight.
options.consequence: A target for playback, treated as a rule for the sound.

options.label: Remaster it yourself tonight
options.result: Ottilie: “Then it's your master, not mine. Good luck with Esme.”
options.consequence: Overrides the people who own the sound.
options.fail: The master's sound is the mastering engineer's and the artist's.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #97 · AVERY'S LENS  Compare at the loudness people will hear  Playback services turn every track to the same loudness. Judge masters loudness-matched, keep true peaks below the delivery limit, and let the people who own the sound choose.  A master pushed to −7 LUFS was turned down 7 dB by the playlist — and next to a quieter, more dynamic master it sounded smaller.

items.alt: The loudness sheet with the chosen master: −11 LUFS, turned down 3 dB to the target; on the right its short-term loudness in green, choruses lifting above verses, over the old flat pink line; true peak −1.0 dBTP.
items.caption: It breathes.

items.title: ‘using all the bits’
items.body: A screenshot on Pim's phone from the choir session: every input peak meter pinned red, captioned ‘using all the bits!!’ Two of those takes are on the album.

items.prompt: What catches the next hot master — and the next clipped take — before the label does?
items.risk: Damage found at mastering, when it can't be fixed.
timeout: The next clipped take is found at mastering.

options.label: Pim promises to be careful
options.result: He is — until the next busy day.

options.label: Loudness and true-peak metering on the master bus, a clip log on every input checked at the end of every session, and a record-level rule on the session sheet: peaks around −10 dBFS
options.result: The first log catches a clipped tambourine on Thursday, the same afternoon.
options.consequence: Watch the numbers that matter, every session.

options.label: Pim listens back to every take for clipping at the end of the day
options.result: He catches most of them. The quiet ones slip through.
options.consequence: The best you can do without the tools — ears on everything, every day.

options.label: A limiter on every input so nothing can clip
options.result: Nothing clips. Everything is squashed before it's recorded.
options.consequence: Damages every take to protect a few.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the delivery week yourself.

items.alt: The control room; Pim holds up the new clip log; Corbin, relaxed for once, with his phone.

bubbles.text: Session-end clip log: zero. And one tambourine re-done on Thursday.
I played both masters to the label, matched. They picked Ottilie's.

items.alt: The live room; an old, well-worn valve guitar amplifier on the floor; Esme stands beside it with her hand over her heart; Maya listens.

bubbles.text: My dad's amp. It always hummed. I want it on the last song.
Then let's find out why it hums — without touching the plug.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Playback services play everything at their own loudness, so a louder master is just turned down further (G = target − measured). Measure integrated loudness and true peak, compare versions at matched loudness, keep true peaks under the delivery limit, and take the evidence to the people who own the sound. Record with room: peaks around −10 dBFS at 24 bits lose nothing; a clipped take is lost for good.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What are you making “louder” that the world will simply turn down?
